before: Two participants who split one paragraph at different points at the same time each listed a new paragraph right after it, and Yjs ordered the new paragraphs by client ID. When the paragraph that holds the later tail came first, a moved copy showed in the last paragraph that held it, so the earlier tail showed in the later paragraph, the earlier paragraph showed nothing, and one split looked lost. The order of concurrent split siblings read only the text each new paragraph copies. When a paragraph of such a run was deleted, a paragraph split off it that held other text could move after its sibling. Concurrent tracked splits of one paragraph each wrote their proposed paragraph mark on the paragraph they split, so the merged paragraph showed one proposal, the other new paragraph mark showed none, and Reject All left a split. Two splits by each of two peers, a break at a paragraph's end beside a split, and siblings an undo or redo listed again could show out of text order with an empty paragraph. Rejecting a proposed paragraph mark joined the paragraph into the one after it and kept the second paragraph's node. An undo of the split that proposed the mark removes the second paragraph instead. When one participant rejected a tracked split while its author undid it, each edit removed the paragraph the other kept, and every replica lost the whole paragraph. A tracked deletion struck every character inside its range, also characters a peer typed there at the same time, so a peer's concurrent typing showed inside the proposed deletion, and Accept All removed it. A caret whose neighbor character a peer deleted moved to the next live character. Beside blocks a peer moved, an undone join could leave one embedded tab twice in shared text, so a later delete was refused as out of bounds; a character a join copied out of a deleted paragraph could show twice; and an undo of typing a peer's split had already moved could show the typing again. An undo of an edit that listed a paragraph, such as a split, removed the paragraph's listing entry, and characters another participant typed there showed nowhere unless they stood beside a moved character whose copy showed elsewhere. When the split's source paragraph was deleted, the undo put the moved text back into that deleted paragraph, where it showed nowhere. A copy that an undo or redo wrote of typed text showed where Yjs placed it, so a redo of typing beside text a peer's split moved showed the typing in the paragraph the text came from, and a redo of typing into a paragraph a peer deleted showed it after the moved text.
after: Paragraphs that a parent lists side by side and that a split added concurrently at one place show in text order. An entry counts as a split's only when the paragraph's split points (collab-split-points) name that entry; a block that a move, an undo, or a redo lists again, and a paragraph without split points, takes no part, so two moves to one place show where their authors put them. Each split's paragraph goes by where the first character its split moved stands in the text it came from; when split points do not decide, paragraphs go by the text they copy: the paragraph whose first copied character comes first in its source text comes first, and when that text is deleted, a paragraph that holds the first character another one copied, after characters of its own, comes first. A paragraph listed later right after one of them, such as a paragraph split off it, moves with it, and only split paragraphs decide where its block shows. A block that an edit moves right after a sibling the rule moves takes that sibling's split points, and when an edit removes such a sibling's entry, the block listed after it from its place takes them, so it keeps the sibling's place. A run that moves nothing leaves its blocks as listed, and a run inside one of them is read on its own. A block whose entries are all removed shows nothing, so the others order past it. The materializer, the projection of local edits, and the document order that decides where a moved copy shows read this one rule; the projection orders a child it lists right after a moved sibling with that sibling for the rest of the edit. So when two participants split one paragraph at different points at the same time, the new paragraphs show in text order, and later edits land where they show. Each replica reads the order again when the parent's child array changes, even when its ids keep their order, and while a paragraph of the run waits for its text or a named split character. A paragraph that a split creates records, in its shared record field splitPoints, the listing entry it was written for, the paragraph it split, and the identity of the first character it moved, after the split points of the paragraph it split (at most four); any other paragraph an edit creates, as a break at a paragraph's end, takes the split points of the paragraph listed right before it. A block that an edit moves right after a concurrent split sibling the order moves takes that sibling's split points, and when an edit removes such a sibling's entry, the block listed after it from its place takes them, so it keeps the sibling's place. The order counts a paragraph as a split only at the entry its field names, so a block a move, an undo, or a redo lists again takes no part where it now stands. The order of concurrent split siblings compares the nearest split of one paragraph two blocks both name, by where those first moved characters stand in the text they came from, and reads the copied text only when they name none in common or the same character. A paragraph split off a deleted sibling keeps that sibling's place. Each proposed paragraph mark a concurrent split wrote shows on the paragraph shown right before that split's new paragraph: the materializer shows it there and the projection of a local edit lists it there before the edit addresses either paragraph. Paragraphs of a run of concurrent splits, each peer's later splits of its own new paragraphs included, order by where each one's own last split fell when those characters all stand in one live text, and otherwise by their split of the paragraph the run follows, a break at a paragraph's end records a split at that end, and a sibling an undo or redo lists again right before its own removed entry in a run belongs to the run; a paragraph listed there anew, whose record its first entry brought, shows where its author put it. A redo that puts back a moved copy, as a redo of a split does, marks it as a moved copy again besides the restore mark, so it shows by document order among the moved copies of its characters and does not hide behind a copy a peer split off at the same time. Split points are written only by the edit that creates the paragraph. Reject All restores the paragraph. The tests cover two peers with up to three typed breaks or Paragraph.split calls each, a single call with two split points, three peers with one split each, one peer undoing and redoing online, and both peers undoing and then redoing offline: every piece shows in text order. Rejecting a proposed paragraph mark keeps the first paragraph, with its node ID and attributes, the properties of the mark that remains, and the content of every joined paragraph in order, as a join by deleting a mark keeps the paragraph before it. The first paragraph is kept when it brings content, or when it held none before the decision, as a break at a paragraph's start leaves; a paragraph the decision emptied goes, and the paragraph after it keeps its identity. A rejection and an undo of the same split both keep the first paragraph, so its text survives on every replica, also when a third participant types in the second paragraph. Accepting a deleted paragraph mark keeps the paragraph after it, as before, and an emptied paragraph keeps its bookmarks and comment starts in the paragraph that stays. Paragraph objects of the second paragraph stop resolving after a rejection. A tracked deletion strikes only the characters its author saw. Each new deletion or move-from value records, in key s, one past the last clock it struck for each client in the struck range (at most 256 clients); readers leave a later character of that client out of the strike and show it with the live text element. A caret whose neighbor character a peer deleted stays where the deleted text was. An embed that shared text holds twice shows once, at its first copy, in both the materializer and the projection of local edits. A deleted paragraph does not bring along a copied character that another paragraph holds. An undo of typing records the deleted characters of the step that stand in paragraph text, so copies a peer writes later stay hidden. A block whose first listed paragraph no split listed there takes no part in the order: a paragraph split off that paragraph tells where it goes after it, not where the block goes. Before an undo runs, the undoing replica records on each paragraph the step listed, in its shared record field undoneInto, where the undo joins that paragraph's text: the nearest paragraph before it that the step did not list, or, with a leading '^', the start of the nearest paragraph after it. While the paragraph is unlisted and not deleted, characters in it that follow no other move show at the end of that paragraph, or at its start, also when they arrive after the undo. When every paragraph a step deleted text from is deleted, its undo keeps each paragraph the step listed that holds moved copies: the listing entry, the record fields, such as the split points, and the copies stay, and text the step typed still goes. A copy that an undo or redo wrote of typed text that stood in the same paragraph text follows a move as the typing did: by the typing's follow anchor, or by the deleted characters it went in after.

A room created with repairVersion 2 keeps the earlier rules, because only replicas with that version edit it. The rule reads shared state and writes nothing, so no stored field or identity changes. A replica can lack part of that state while updates are on their way: a split point can name a character it has not received. It then orders that run by what it holds, and reads the run again when the character arrives. The clock order of one author decides only when the replica holds both characters and they do not stand in one live text, so every replica that holds the same updates shows the same order, whatever the arrival order and with garbage collection on or off. Tracked concurrent splits still keep one of the proposed paragraph marks on the split paragraph, so one proposed break has no revision and Reject All leaves it; two splits by each peer in one paragraph, a break at the end with a split in the middle, and a redo after both undos are not settled yet. The field is a new key on a paragraph record. The edit that creates the paragraph writes it, in the transaction that lists the paragraph. An edit that moves a block right after a concurrent split sibling the order moves, or that removes such a sibling's entry, writes it again on the block that takes the sibling's place, also on a record another participant created. Each value names the listing entry it belongs to, so every replica reads the same value alike, whichever edit wrote it last. Released readers would not read it and would order the run by text alone, which is the repairVersion 3 change these records already make; replicas with repairVersion 2 refuse these rooms. A paragraph without the field, as a release without it wrote, falls back to the text rule, so rooms of this format created before the field order as before. sharedSchemaVersion does not change: the field is an optional key that only replicas of this format write and read, no existing field changes meaning, and a paragraph without it orders by the earlier rule. Where a proposal shows and which paragraphs a run holds are rules over the same shared state, so they belong to repairVersion 3, which these records already introduce; replicas with repairVersion 2 refuse these rooms. The projection moves a proposal with ordinary child splices, as merged property copies and adoption already do. A redo of a moved copy writes one more text mark, of a kind every replica of this format already reads; no field changes. The survivor of a rejected paragraph mark decides which conflicting node survives a concurrent undo or a concurrent equal decision, so it is repair semantics. A replica with repairVersion 2 keeps the second paragraph; in one room with this version, two concurrent rejections of one proposed mark each remove the paragraph the other keeps, and the paragraph is lost. repairVersion increases to 3, so the two versions refuse to share a room before any update applies, and a room created with repairVersion 2 keeps the earlier rule. The journal writes ordinary moves, removals, and text copies; no stored field changes. The s key is a new key in a revision attribute value that only replicas of this format write and read. A replica with repairVersion 2 would strike a peer's concurrent characters, so the two would show other text for one state; repairVersion 3 already makes them refuse to share a room. A value without s, as earlier rooms of this format hold, strikes its whole range as before. Client keys and clocks are validated, and an invalid s is ignored. The rules for moved blocks read shared state the same way on every replica and write only ordinary deletion records.
